
This vignette reproduces the classical analysis of the `sapi` series (six
calendar variation models fitted to 2004--2024 and tested on 2025), adds
lunarcast to it, and then shows why a single test year is not enough to
compare the two.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(lunarcast)
adha  <- holiday_dates("idul_adha")
fitri <- holiday_dates("idul_fitri")
train <- window(sapi, end = c(2024, 12))
test  <- window(sapi, start = c(2025, 1))
```

## The six classical models

Each model is a regression with ARIMA errors on the original scale with the
Eid al-Adha month dummy $V_t$ and a constant effect $\alpha$:

| Model | Trend | Seasonality |
|:--|:--|:--|
| m1 | deterministic ($\beta_0 + \beta_1 t$) | 11 monthly dummies |
| m2 | deterministic | Fourier terms, $K = 5$ |
| m3 | stochastic (differencing) | 11 monthly dummies |
| m4 | stochastic | Fourier terms, $K = 5$ |
| m5 | deterministic | seasonal ARIMA |
| m6 | stochastic | seasonal ARIMA |

```{r classic}
classic <- calvar_classic_all(train, adha)
classic
```

The column `effect` is the constant holiday effect $\alpha$ in index points.
The estimates differ slightly from an analysis whose dummy omits the second
Eid al-Adha of 2006 (31 December); `holiday_dates()` includes both.
It is much smaller in m5 and m6 than in m1 to m4: with seasonal ARIMA errors,
part of the holiday effect is carried by the seasonal autoregression instead
of the dummy. With monthly dummies, part of it is absorbed by the dummy of
the months in which the holiday often fell.

## lunarcast on the same data

```{r lunarcast}
lc <- lunarcast(train, list(adha = adha, fitri = fitri))
lc
```

## One test year: 2025

```{r test}
fc_classic <- forecast(classic, h = length(test))
fc_lc      <- forecast(lc, h = length(test))
acc <- do.call(forecast_accuracy,
               c(list(actual = test), fc_classic, list(lunarcast = fc_lc)))
acc[, -1] <- round(acc[, -1], 2)
acc
```

```{r test-plot}
plot(test, ylim = c(0, max(test, fc_lc$mean) * 1.15), lwd = 2, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Index", main = "2025: observed and forecasts")
lines(fc_classic$m6$mean, col = "darkorange", lwd = 1.5)
lines(fc_lc$mean, col = "royalblue", lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("observed", "classical m6", "lunarcast"), bty = "n",
       col = c("grey40", "darkorange", "royalblue"), lwd = c(2, 1.5, 1.5))
```

A single test year is a fragile basis for comparison. In 2025 Eid al-Adha
fell in June for the third year in a row, the ideal situation for a seasonal
ARIMA model, which simply repeats last year's June, so the classical m6 model
also does well. The difficult years are those in which the holiday moves to
another month, and they do not occur every year.

## Fourteen test years: rolling origin

`rolling_origin()` refits every model at the end of each year from 2011 to
2024 and forecasts the following year, so that 14 test years (2012 to 2025,
167 months) are used. Running it for all models takes some time; the results
for `sapi` are stored in the package:

```{r rolling-read}
r <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "rolling_sapi.csv", package = "lunarcast"))
r$model <- factor(r$model, levels = unique(r$model))
rolling_summary(r)
```

The lunarcast rows differ only in how the seasonal structure is chosen: by
AICc (`lunarcast_aicc`), fixed without seasonality (`lunarcast_none`) or by
cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule (`lunarcast`, the
default). The code that produced the file is shown at the
end of this vignette.

```{r rolling-plot}
yearly <- tapply((r$pred - r$actual)^2, list(r$year, r$model),
                 function(v) sqrt(mean(v)))
years <- as.numeric(rownames(yearly))
plot(years, yearly[, "classic_m6"], type = "b", pch = 19, col = "darkorange",
     ylim = c(0, max(yearly[, c("classic_m6", "lunarcast")]) * 1.1),
     xlab = "", ylab = "RMSE", main = "RMSE per test year")
lines(years, yearly[, "lunarcast"], type = "b", pch = 19, col = "royalblue")
legend("topleft", c("classical m6", "lunarcast"), col = c("darkorange", "royalblue"),
       pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

What the table shows:

* The best classical model is m6 (stochastic trend and seasonality). The
  models with seasonal dummies or Fourier terms (m1 to m4) are clearly worse,
  because the dummies of the months in which the holiday used to fall keep
  predicting peaks after the holiday has moved.
* lunarcast lowers the overall RMSE from 7.95 to 4.94 and the RMSE in
  holiday months from 20.25 to 8.30 (about 60%).
* Choosing the structure by AICc picks seasonal ARIMA errors at most origins
  and gives a clearly worse forecast than cross-validation: a good in-sample
  fit is not the same as a good forecast.

## How the rolling-origin results were produced

```{r produce, eval = FALSE}
hol  <- list(adha = adha, fitri = fitri)
spec <- classic$spec
classic_models <- lapply(seq_len(6), function(i) {
  force(i)
  function(y, h) forecast(calvar_classic(y, adha, spec$trend[i], spec$season[i]),
                          h = h)$mean
})
names(classic_models) <- paste0("classic_", spec$model)

# the lunarcast variants share the calendar selected at each origin
lunarcast_variant <- function(...) {
  function(y, h) {
    base <- lunarcast(y, hol, select = "aicc")
    fit  <- lunarcast(y, hol, window = base$window, effect = base$effect, ...)
    forecast(fit, h = h)$mean
  }
}
lunarcast_models <- list(
  lunarcast_aicc = function(y, h) forecast(lunarcast(y, hol, select = "aicc"), h = h)$mean,
  lunarcast_none = lunarcast_variant(season = "none", select = "aicc"),
  lunarcast      = lunarcast_variant()
)
r <- rolling_origin(sapi, adha, c(classic_models, lunarcast_models), first = 2012)
rolling_summary(r)
```

The same code is in `data-raw/rolling_sapi.R` in the package repository.
